learningObjectives.title: Peacemaking: the armistice and the Treaty of Versailles
The League of Nations and international peace in the 1920s
The collapse of the League of Nations in the 1930s
The origins and outbreak of the Second World War

questions.q: On what date did the armistice that ended the fighting of the First World War come into effect?
questions.explain: The armistice between the Allies and Germany came into force at 11am on 11 November 1918.

questions.q: On what date was the Treaty of Versailles signed?
questions.explain: The Treaty of Versailles was signed on 28 June 1919 in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles.

questions.q: Which leader represented France as one of the 'Big Three' at the Paris Peace Conference?
questions.explain: Georges Clemenceau, nicknamed 'the Tiger', represented France alongside Wilson of the USA and Lloyd George of Britain.

questions.q: Which statement best describes Georges Clemenceau's main aim at the peace conference?
options: To weaken Germany and guarantee French security
To create a League of Nations based on self-determination
To avoid punishing Germany harshly in order to protect trade
questions.explain: Having seen France invaded twice, Clemenceau wanted Germany crippled and permanent security for France.

questions.q: Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles is commonly known as the:
questions.explain: Article 231, the War Guilt Clause, forced Germany to accept full responsibility for causing the war.

questions.q: Which term of the Treaty of Versailles was designed mainly to protect France by creating a buffer zone on Germany's western border?
options: The return of Alsace-Lorraine to France
The ban on a German air force
questions.explain: The Rhineland was demilitarised so that German troops could not mass on France's border, acting as a buffer zone.

questions.q: A German newspaper in 1919 attacks the treaty as a 'Diktat'. Which point best explains why Germans used this term?
options: Germany was forced to accept the terms without any negotiation
Germany helped to write the treaty at Versailles
Germany kept all of its overseas colonies
The treaty was approved by a German referendum
questions.explain: 'Diktat' means a dictated peace: Germany was excluded from the talks and made to sign under threat of invasion.

questions.q: Where was the permanent headquarters of the League of Nations located?
questions.explain: The League of Nations was based in Geneva in neutral Switzerland.

questions.q: Which major power, despite its President having proposed it, never joined the League of Nations?
questions.explain: Although Woodrow Wilson championed the League, the US Senate refused to ratify it and the USA never joined.

questions.q: What did the Corfu incident of 1923 reveal about the League of Nations?
options: A great power could defy the League and be backed by the Conference of Ambassadors
The League could reliably stop aggression by great powers
It was the League's greatest success of the decade
It led directly to Italy leaving the League
questions.explain: Mussolini's Italy occupied Corfu, and the Conference of Ambassadors overruled the League, forcing Greece to pay compensation.

questions.q: In 1921 the League settled a dispute between Sweden and Finland over the Aaland Islands. How is this case best used in an exam answer?
options: As a genuine success, since the League peacefully settled the dispute in Finland's favour
As a failure, since Sweden went to war over the islands
As proof the League only worked against great powers
As an example of economic sanctions forcing Sweden to back down
questions.explain: Both sides accepted the League's ruling that the islands remain Finnish, showing peaceful arbitration could work.

questions.q: In which year did Japan invade the Chinese region of Manchuria?
questions.explain: Japan invaded Manchuria in 1931, using the Mukden incident as a pretext.

questions.q: Why did the Manchurian Crisis (1931-33) damage the League of Nations?
options: It showed the League could not stop a major power, which then simply left the League
It proved that economic sanctions always worked
It was quickly resolved by the League's own army
It persuaded the USA to join the League
questions.explain: After the Lytton Report condemned Japan, Japan ignored it and left the League in 1933, exposing the League's weakness.

questions.q: Why is the Abyssinian Crisis of 1935-36 often described as the event that 'killed' the League of Nations?
options: A leading League member conquered another member state despite sanctions
The League successfully defended Abyssinia from invasion
Abyssinia had never been a member of the League
The USA vetoed all League action over Abyssinia
questions.explain: Mussolini's Italy, a permanent Council member, overran Abyssinia while limited sanctions and an open Suez Canal failed to stop it.

questions.q: Why did the Hoare-Laval Pact of 1935 damage the League of Nations?
options: Two leading members secretly plotted to hand much of Abyssinia to Italy
It closed the Suez Canal to Italian ships
It imposed a total oil ban on Italy
It expelled Britain from the League
questions.explain: British and French ministers secretly planned to give Italy large parts of Abyssinia, undermining the League's principles when leaked.

questions.q: Why was Hitler's remilitarisation of the Rhineland in March 1936 significant?
options: It broke the Treaty of Versailles and Locarno, yet Britain and France took no action
It was fully permitted under the Treaty of Versailles
It triggered an immediate French invasion of Germany
It was carried out on the orders of the League of Nations
questions.explain: Sending troops into the Rhineland violated both Versailles and Locarno, but the lack of Allied response emboldened Hitler.

questions.q: The Munich Agreement of September 1938, which let Germany take the Sudetenland, is the clearest example of which policy?
questions.explain: Britain and France gave in to Hitler's demands over the Sudetenland to avoid war, the classic act of appeasement.

questions.q: In which month and year was the Nazi-Soviet Pact signed?
questions.explain: The Nazi-Soviet Pact was signed in August 1939, with a secret clause to divide Poland.

questions.q: Returning from Munich in 1938, Chamberlain declared he had secured 'peace for our time'. Which event most clearly proved him wrong?
options: Germany occupied the rest of Czechoslovakia in March 1939
Germany rejoined the League of Nations
questions.explain: Hitler's seizure of the rest of Czechoslovakia in March 1939 broke the Munich promise and discredited appeasement.

questions.q: Britain and France declared war on Germany on 3 September 1939 as a direct result of which action?
options: The signing of the Munich Agreement
questions.explain: Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939, and honouring their guarantee to Poland, Britain and France declared war two days later.

specSource: AQA GCSE History (8145) specification; Conflict and Tension, 1918-1939 (Inter-war years)
